title: Why they differ
hook: different reports, readings, and methods, all seeking the same thing

segments.voice: Yesterday, praying behind another, and your line: one row. Did you stand beside someone whose habits weren't yours, and let them be? Day one thousand two hundred fourteen.

One word in the Qur'an, and the schools read it two ways. Surah two, verse two hundred twenty-eight, in Pickthall's translation: "Women who are divorced shall wait, keeping themselves apart, three (monthly) courses." The Arabic word behind those courses is quru'. And quru' can mean the monthly periods themselves. Or it can mean the clean days between them. Same verse. Same Arabic. Same sincerity. The Hanafi and Hanbali schools count the periods. The Maliki and Shafi'i schools count the clean intervals. Nobody skipped the verse. They all read it, carefully, and the word itself held two doors open. Today: why they differ.
screen: `THREE (MONTHLY) COURSES.` → `QURU': PERIODS, OR THE DAYS BETWEEN?` → `ONE VERSE, TWO HONEST READINGS.`

segments.voice: So that's the first reason: readings. Arabic words can carry more than one meaning, and the schools sometimes chose differently. Second, reports. Not every hadith reached every scholar. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps a story about Umar, the caliph. Abu Musa came to his door, asked permission three times, heard no answer, and left. Umar called him back and asked why. Abu Musa said the Prophet ﷺ had taught that: ask three times, and if there's no answer, go. Umar had never heard it, and he wanted a witness. Abu Sa'id stood up and confirmed it. And Umar said, in meaning, that trading in the markets had kept him busy. If the caliph could miss a report, so could a scholar in another city. Third, methods. Once the reports are in hand, how do you weigh them? Imam Malik gave weight to the living practice of the people of Medina. Other schools leaned more on analogy, or on a lone report with a strong chain. Each method is a way of being careful. Ibn Taymiyya later wrote a short book, Raf' al-Malam, the removal of blame from the great imams, to explain why a sound scholar might leave a hadith aside: it hadn't reached him, he doubted its chain, or he read it another way. Fourth, what they share. In Bukhari, the Prophet says that when a judge strives and gets it right, he has two rewards, and when he strives and gets it wrong, he has one. The striving itself is rewarded. That closes this stretch on how the schools differ: hands, amin, touch and wudu, the moon, witr, other schools, the row. Underneath every one, the same search.
screen: `ONE WORD, TWO MEANINGS.` · `A REPORT THAT DIDN'T REACH HIM.` · `DIFFERENT WAYS OF WEIGHING.` · `TWO REWARDS, OR ONE.`

segments.voice: The practice: respect a sincere difference. Settle, and let the breath go long. Bring to mind one person who disagrees with you about something that matters, a person you know to be honest. Not the loudest voice online. Someone real. Picture them at their kitchen table, working it out, the way you work things out. Ask what they might have read, or heard, or weighed that you haven't. You don't have to change your mind. Just let them be someone who is seeking too. If you pray, you can remember them kindly in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Why they differ. Different readings of a word, different reports that reached them, different methods of weighing, all seeking the same thing. Today's word.
Your line: seeking the same. Today, when someone disagrees with you, ask one honest question about how they got there before you answer. Day one thousand two hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Muslim students of law learn not only their school's rulings but the reasons schools differ, such as a word with two meanings, a report that reached one scholar and not another, or a different way of weighing evidence.

fork.setup: you're Umar. a companion says the Prophet taught a rule you've never heard. what do you do?
options: dismiss it: you would have heard.
ask for a witness, and accept it when one comes.
ignore it and keep your own practice.
fork.reveal: Umar asked for a witness. Abu Sa'id confirmed it, and Umar said that trading in the markets had kept him busy.

original.note: Arabic: the word in 2:228; some schools read it as monthly periods, others as the clean intervals between them.

trapdoor: what you thought: if scholars differ, someone must be careless.
what it means: they differ over words with two meanings, reports that reached some and not others, and how to weigh them.
what a scholar hears: Ibn Taymiyya's Raf' al-Malam, a defense of the great imams explaining why a sound scholar might leave a hadith aside.
